hypothesis: The neuron responds selectively to small-to-medium sized, highly saturated, rounded objects—typically spheres, discs, or convex ovals—appearing as distinct spots of vivid color. The activating features are consistently colored in intense, high-chroma hues such as neon chartreuse/lime green, scarlet or coral red, bright orange, hot pink, or lemon yellow. These colorful forms usually possess a smooth or fuzzy texture (e.g., tennis balls, rose hips, berries, buttons, or plastic decals) and are set against backgrounds that are either neutral (grey, concrete, beige) or of a contrasting natural tone (such as a green object on red clay, or a red object on green foliage), creating a strong chromatic pop. The feature typically occupies 10–40% of the image area and is positioned centrally or slightly off-center. The neuron is invariant to the object's specific semantic identity (biological vs. synthetic) and surface material, provided the strong saturation, rounded form, and figure-ground color contrast are maintained.
